name: The British Raj
title: Social Hierarchy of British India: From Viceroy to Indentured Labourer

tiers.name: The viceroy
tiers.you: You govern India from Calcutta in the Crown’s name, with a council of department heads, but every law made in India needs the assent of the Secretary of State in London.
tiers.kid: The viceroy ruled India for the British queen or king, who lived far away in Britain.
tiers.rise: The Crown appointed him, for no fixed term though typically for five years. Curzon resigned in 1905 after a dispute with his military chief, Lord Kitchener.
tiers.why: After 1858 the governor-general of India was more commonly called the viceroy, from his second role as the Crown’s representative to the princely states.

tiers.name: British officials and residents
tiers.you: You passed the examination in London and now help govern a district of hundreds of thousands of people; you are British, as almost every Civilian is, and your pay is many times that of the Indians in government service.
tiers.kid: A small group of British officials, chosen by exams held in London, ran the districts of British India.
tiers.rise: A candidate had to be aged 18 to 23 and pass a horse-riding test; after probation at Oxford, Cambridge, London or Dublin, an Assistant Commissioner began on about £300 a year, served at least 25 years and retired on a pension of £1,000. The examination was at first held only in London; from 1922 Indian candidates could sit it in Delhi.
tiers.why: British control in the districts rested on the Indian Civil Service (ICS), whose members, the “Civilians”, were at first almost all British and educated in the best British schools.

tiers.name: The princes
tiers.you: You are a maharaja whose rank is fixed by the number of guns fired in your salute; you keep your own courts, but a British resident watches over you, and you may not deal with any foreign power.
tiers.kid: Indian princes still ruled hundreds of states, big and small, but Britain controlled their armies and their dealings with other countries.
tiers.rise: A prince inherited his throne, but the British could grant or withhold recognition. The doctrine of lapse, under which the East India Company had annexed states whose ruler died without a natural heir, ended in 1858. Princes who had kept out of the rebellion of 1857 had their territories guaranteed, and their sons were schooled at Mayo College and Aitchison College on the model of the English public schools.
tiers.why: Nearly 600 princely states, covering 40 per cent of the land and 23 per cent of its people in 1947, were ruled by Indian princes under British paramountcy.

tiers.name: Zamindars and great landholders
tiers.you: You hold a great estate in Bengal under the Permanent Settlement; you owe the government a fixed rent, and if you fail to pay it by sunset part of your land will be sold at auction.
tiers.kid: Zamindars were rich landowners who paid the government a fixed sum each year for their great estates.
tiers.rise: An estate passed by descent or adoption, and a lawfully wedded wife could inherit it if the zamindar named her heir; the British rewarded some supportive zamindars by recognising them as princes. Because many peasants had fought for their former landlords in 1857, the British made no more land reforms for 90 years, and Bengal and Bihar remained realms of large landholdings.
tiers.why: The zamindars held the great estates of the north and east.

tiers.name: Brahmins
tiers.you: You were born a Brahmin; the census ranks your jati near the top of its tables, and the government’s offices are open to men of your caste.
tiers.kid: Brahmins were the priestly caste, ranked highest in old Hindu writings, and the British gave government jobs to the upper castes.
tiers.rise: Birth into a Brahmin jati decided it. Lower castes sought Brahmin or Kshatriya status for whole communities, a process called Sanskritisation; the upper castes had resisted such claims before British rule, but they spread under it.
tiers.why: The varna scheme of the ancient texts placed the Brahmins, the priests, at the head of four orders, above the Kshatriyas (rulers and warriors), the Vaishyas (traders) and the Shudras (labourers), with Dalits and…

tiers.name: The educated middle class
tiers.you: You took a degree in law at the University of Bombay and practise at the bar; you resent the racial discrimination of the British and have joined the new Indian National Congress.
tiers.kid: Indians who studied at the new universities became lawyers and officials, and some started the Indian National Congress.
tiers.rise: Education was the way in: matriculation, a degree in arts or law, and a post in the administration or at the bar. Few climbed higher, since almost all the top posts went to Britons, typically with an Oxford or Cambridge degree.
tiers.why: By 1880 a new middle class had arisen across the country.

tiers.name: Merchants, bankers and moneylenders
tiers.you: You lend money to small farmers who grow for export; when the market falls they pay you in land, animals and tools, though in the north-west a law of 1900 now bars land from passing to castes not listed as agricultural.
tiers.kid: Merchants and bankers traded and lent money, and some Indians built cotton mills and a great steelworks.
tiers.rise: Wealth could buy land, but in the north-west the Land Alienation Act of 1900 listed the castes that could own land and barred its transfer to non-agricultural castes. The reforms of 1909 favoured rich landowners and businessmen, and those of 1919 reserved seats for businessmen.
tiers.why: In the varna scheme trade belonged to the Vaishyas.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You till your fields and pay the land tax on which the government lives; in the famine of 1899–1900 millions around you die.
tiers.kid: Most Indians were farmers who paid taxes on their land, and millions died when terrible famines came.
tiers.rise: Peasant castes tried to rise as groups: under British rule pastoral communities such as the Ahirs took the name Yadav, and tilling castes such as the Kurmis formed caste associations claiming higher status. In 1917 Gandhi took up the cause of tenant farmers in Champaran, forced to grow indigo for British planters.
tiers.why: Most Indians were peasants, the ryots, living at subsistence level.

tiers.name: Artisans, mill hands and labourers
tiers.you: You work for low wages in an Indian-owned cotton mill in Ahmedabad, and in 1918 you join the strike that Gandhi supports with a fast.
tiers.kid: Many weavers lost their work to cheap British cloth, while others worked in new cotton mills and on the railways.
tiers.rise: Weavers and ironworkers lost their trades to imports, while others found work in the mills and on the railways, where Indians were kept to unskilled work: in 1920 they held only ten per cent of the railways’ superior posts.
tiers.why: Cheap British cloth, imported under the “free trade” Britain imposed on India, shrank its largest industry: imports of cotton cloth rose from about a million yards in 1814 to 2,050 million in 1890, and by 1870–1880…

tiers.name: Castes treated as untouchable
tiers.you: You were born into a caste the others call untouchable: you may not draw water from the well the higher castes use, and they will not take food or drink from your hands.
tiers.kid: People of the castes called untouchable were kept apart, even at the village well, and reformers like Ambedkar fought for their rights.
tiers.rise: Birth decided it, and conversion did not undo it: in Kerala the Protestant Dalit Christians of the missions were still treated as lower castes. B. R. Ambedkar, born into a caste classified as untouchable, became a leader of human-rights campaigns; at his request the Communal Award of 1932 gave the depressed classes separate electorates, which he gave up in the Poona Pact after Gandhi’s hunger strike.
tiers.why: Outside the four varnas stood the communities treated as untouchable, the Dalits.

tiers.name: Castes and tribes declared criminal
tiers.you: Your caste is on the government’s list of criminal tribes: although you have been convicted of nothing, the law limits where you may go and with whom you may mix.
tiers.kid: A British law of 1871 labelled whole castes as born criminals and limited where their members could go.
tiers.rise: Birth and the census register decided it. The practice was disputed among British officials, and in a few cases it was reversed early in the 20th century on the ground that people “could not be incarcerated indefinitely on the presumption of [inherited] bad character”; elsewhere the lists grew through the 1930s.
tiers.why: The Criminal Tribes Act of 1871 declared that all who belonged to certain castes were born with criminal tendencies.

tiers.name: Indentured labourers
tiers.you: You signed on in Calcutta and now cut cane on a sugar estate in British Guiana, six days a week for a shilling a day; if you are absent from work, you can be sent to prison.
tiers.kid: Many poor Indians were sent to work on sugar farms on faraway islands, often after being tricked by recruiters.
tiers.rise: A recruit had to appear before a magistrate of his district, and a free passage home came only after ten years’ residence. Labourers resisted by slowdowns, strikes, sabotage and desertion; many stayed, and Trinidad gave five acres and £5 to those who gave up their passage. Indenture to Natal ended in 1911, after Gokhale’s bill, and to the other colonies in 1917.
tiers.why: From 1834, when the ship Atlas carried 36 labourers from Calcutta to Mauritius, more than 1.6 million Indians were shipped to European colonies whose planters wanted cheap labour after slavery was abolished, from…
